item.title: Ultra-precise coatings help power the next generation of gravitational wave detectors
item.description: Researchers from The Australian National University (ANU) have engineered new optical coatings for LIGO, the global collaboration hunting gravitational waves from colliding black holes and neutron stars. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: How North Korean defectors help us understand refugee entrepreneurs
item.description: Refugees are more likely than native citizens to begin entrepreneurial ventures in their adopted countries, either by choice or because they have few other options. A new study offers insight into how refugees from common backgrounds end up adopting very different approaches to running their businesses by focusing on refugees who defected from North Korea and started their own ventures in South Korea. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Desert alga reveals how fast growth and resistance to extreme conditions can coexist
item.description: A single-celled green alga from the sand dunes of the Negev Desert has, within just a few years, become a key model organism in modern photosynthesis research. Chlorella ohadii helps researchers better understand plants' adaptability to extreme environmental conditions. These findings could help make crops more resilient to heat, drought, and other consequences of climate change in the future. Haim Treves, a professor of plant metabolism at RPTU, has been studying the desert alga since its discovery. His findings have now been published in the journal New Phytologist. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: NASA’s SpaceX Crew-13 Launches
item.description: In this Oct. 1, 2026, photo, a SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket and Dragon spacecraft launch from Space Launch Complex 40 at Cape Canaveral Space Force Station in Florida. The spacecraft is carrying NASA astronauts Jessica Watkins and Luke Delaney, CSA (Canadian Space Agency) astronaut Joshua Kutryk, and Roscosmos cosmonaut Sergey Teteryatnikov to the International Space Station for a […] Fuente: NASA.

item.title: True identity emerges from lived experience, not hidden essence, research finds
item.description: So, you're a people pleaser? A social chameleon? Perhaps you're an introvert or an extrovert. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Viral enzyme cuts bacterial sensor protein, triggering defense against invading phages
item.description: In the fight to find better treatments for bacterial infections, one rapidly evolving therapy uses a group of viruses called bacteriophages (phages). Phages can attack and kill dangerous bacteria while leaving human cells unharmed and bypassing antibiotic resistance. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Precisely patterned molecular threads boost neuron growth and synapse formation in cell cultures
item.description: Northwestern University scientists have developed remarkably long, precisely patterned molecular threads that could open new possibilities for designing advanced materials. The scientists also discovered that these threads—called supramolecular polymers—can dramatically enhance brain cell activity. The study is published in the journal Science. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: China linked hackers pose as former US officials to steal emails from researchers, Proofpoint says
item.description: Chinese hackers have been impersonating US AI experts to steal emails from AI experts at think tanks and universities. Fuente: The Jerusalem Post - International.
item.dc:creator: BY REUTERS

item.title: Growth in milk boosts Staph bacteria's resistance to antibiotics, experiments reveal
item.description: Staphylococcus aureus is frequently found in human and veterinary infections. It is named for the golden-yellow pigment it produces, which contributes to its virulence and protects it against oxidative stress. Its ability to withstand antibiotic treatment makes it a major clinical challenge. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Sea change: WildFin aims to improve fish behavior analysis in the wild
item.description: In the first year of her doctoral research, Abigail Grassick collected hours of underwater video as she studied fish communities living on bommies—individual clumps of coral—on the seafloor off the coast of Curaçao. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Fluent in two languages? It comes at a cost to emotional regulation (but don't worry)
item.description: Say "I'm angry" out loud, and your brain reacts to it, reducing the use of emotional brain regions. But this trick does not work if you say it in your second language. A new study published in the journal Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences shows that it doesn't work in any language if you are a balanced bilingual. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: From suicide bombers to positions of authority—the changing role of women in jihadi groups
item.description: Khadra Essa, a Somali-born Dutch citizen operating in Syria under the name Umm Qaqa al-Somali, is a wanted woman. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Teen sexting: Why 'just say no' fails
item.description: Blunt warnings telling teenagers not to share sexual images are failing to protect them and can make victims of image-based sexual abuse feel blamed, ashamed and unable to seek help, according to new research from the University of Surrey. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: What’s Up: October 2026 Skywatching Tips from NASA
item.description: A Meteor Shower and the Moon Near the Pleiades See Saturn at opposition, catch the Orionid meteor shower, and watch the Moon pass close to the Pleiades, also known as the Seven Sisters. Skywatching Highlights Transcript Saturn takes center stage, a meteor shower lights up the sky, and the Moon visits the Seven Sisters. That’s […] Fuente: NASA.

item.title: SpaceX launches 4 astronauts on a fast track to the International Space Station
item.description: Four crew members of NASA’s SpaceX Crew-13 mission launched at 11:10 a.m. EDT Thursday from Space Launch Complex 40 at Cape Canaveral Space Force Station in Florida for a science expedition aboard the International Space Station. “Crew-13 is another demonstration of America’s unmatched capability in human spaceflight and the strength of our commercial partnerships,” said […] Publicado también por: NASA. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Largest-ever jaguar analysis identifies how populations are connected across the Americas
item.description: An international team of researchers has produced the most comprehensive assessment to date of connectivity across the jaguar's range, identifying key habitats and movement corridors that could help guide conservation efforts for the Americas' largest cat. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Celebrity accounts reveal distinctive victim-blaming in deepfake sexual abuse
item.description: Celebrity victim-survivors of deepfake sexual abuse face distinctive forms of victim-blaming, harassment and barriers to justice, according to new research led by Irish researchers. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Urban environments may be the ultimate training grounds for invasive species
item.description: As cities grow and urban sprawl expands, could these changing landscapes be giving invasive species a competitive edge? Scientists at the University of Florida Institute of Food and Agricultural Sciences (UF/IFAS) say the answer may be yes, according to a new study from the UF/IFAS Invasion Science Institute. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Hazelwood redevelopment suggests neighborhood investment can advance without typical displacement pressures
item.description: Neighborhood investments meant to improve housing and opportunity often spark fears of gentrification and displacement. That worry is playing out in Pittsburgh's Hazelwood neighborhood, where a stalled Second Avenue housing project sits blocks from the 178-acre (72-hectare) Hazelwood Green riverfront development. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Sex-like DNA exchange in starving bacteria occurs over 100 times more often than spontaneous mutations
item.description: How do bacteria adapt when resources run low? ISTA researchers have found that, under starvation stress, E. coli can use bacteriophages and CRISPR-Cas immunity to transfer and incorporate DNA, accelerating genetic reshuffling. The process resembles a primitive form of sexual reproduction and may help bacterial populations adapt to changing conditions. The findings were published in Molecular Biology and Evolution. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Does a deeper voice make men more attractive? These researchers have the answer
item.description: During puberty, as boys transition into men, the dramatic drop in their vocal pitch has sparked a long-running debate among scientists. Why did such deep voices evolve in the first place? Was it to attract female mates or to intimidate rival men? Or perhaps something else is going on. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Global health research delivers medical advances and economic benefits far beyond its target countries
item.description: Recently, a middle-aged woman came to see me in my ophthalmology clinic because her eyes felt gritty and uncomfortable. She had seen another doctor a month earlier who diagnosed her with eyelid inflammation and wrote her a prescription. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Ready at 12? Why age alone cannot tell you when children can go out unsupervised
item.description: By the time children are around 12 years old, many will begin to ask if they can go out to the local park, playground or stores to spend time with their friends without adult supervision. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Stable salts unlock alternative to potentially explosive reagents in carbene chemistry
item.description: Many useful reactions in chemistry come with a trade-off: the reactive reagents that make them effective can also present practical and safety challenges. Carbene chemistry is one such example. For decades, chemists have relied on diazo compounds to generate reactive carbenes, even though diazoalkanes can be toxic, unstable and potentially explosive. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: As US relations fray, Canada gets serious about its own launch industry
item.description: The Canada Rocket Company gets serious about medium-lift launch. Fuente: Ars Technica.
item.dc:creator: Eric Berger

item.title: Study finds city-level fire data can hide what's happening block by block
item.description: A decade of New York City fire data shows that citywide trends can mask sharply different realities on the ground, with some neighborhoods moving in the opposite direction of the city as a whole. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Chimps plunder less pineapple from friends—and expect them to do the same
item.description: In recent years, scientists have shown that chimpanzees favor certain peers by picking whom they prefer to groom and selectively sharing food. The behavior offers a glimpse into humanity's prosocial evolutionary past. But a question has lingered: How might a chimpanzee friendship affect antisocial acts? Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Dolphins keep their social and hunting lives in separate waters, study finds
item.description: Dolphins, it turns out, don’t like to mix business and pleasure. Scientists have found that the marine mammals keep their feeding and hunting areas separate from the places where they socialize with one another. A study published in the journal PeerJ details how a team of researchers listened in on dolphins living along the Atlantic […] Fuente: Mongabay.
item.dc:creator: Abhishyantkidangoor

item.title: Underlying causes of recurrent bacterial vaginosis identified by Australian scientists
item.description: Melbourne researchers behind previous BV transmission breakthrough turn attention to understanding why some cases are harder to cure Australian scientists have identified two contributors to recurrent bacterial vaginosis infections, a common sexual health condition that affects about one in four women globally. The condition, commonly called BV, is characterised by an imbalance of naturally occurring bacteria in the vagina, in which there is a reduction of “good” bacteria and an overgrowth of other mixed bacteria. Continue reading... Fuente: The Guardian - World.
item.dc:creator: Donna Lu Assistant editor, climate, environment and science

item.title: Catalog of mitochondria across life's family tree unearths unusual functions
item.description: A research consortium has generated the broadest look yet at the proteins that make up mitochondria, capturing the organelle's diversity across multiple branches on the tree of complex life. With major contributions from Broad Institute scientists and its Proteomics Platform, the consortium generated and analyzed the mitochondrial proteomes of one plant and five single-celled pathogens that affect millions of people globally every year. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Eye-eating amoeba resists treatment—understanding its biochemistry could help
item.description: In water, soil and air all around us lives a free-living, single-celled organism called Acanthamoeba. Most of the time, Acanthamoeba keeps to itself. On rare occasions, though, the amoeba infects humans and can cause severe infections of the eyes, skin and even the brain. What's more, doctors can struggle to diagnose and treat the eye infection caused by the organism, called Acanthamoeba keratitis. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: How going digital offers families more than annual adoption letters
item.description: Digital technology could transform the way adopted children stay connected with their birth families, according to new research from the University of East Anglia. A study published in the journal Adoption & Fostering reveals how a custom-built online platform called Letter Swap offers more modern ways for families to connect by swapping messages, videos, voice notes and photos rather than relying on traditional annual letters. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Following ancient rain toward life-related chemistry clues on Mars
item.description: The Mars we know today is a cold, dry world of dust and rocks. However, around 3.8–3.6 billion years ago, it may have looked very different. Geological and mineral evidence suggests that, in its distant past, the planet experienced periods warm and wet enough for water to exist on its surface, potentially forming rivers, lakes and even an ocean in the northern hemisphere. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: NASA’s Webb Provides Crash Course on Planet-Shattering Collisions
item.description: In the early history of our solar system, scientists theorize that a Mars-sized object called Theia smashed into the infant Earth, vaporizing massive amounts of rock and blasting it into space. Some of that material coalesced into the Moon, where NASA’s Artemis program is returning humans, preparing for Mars, and shaping the future of space […] Fuente: NASA.

item.title: This giant stick insect fooled scientists for decades
item.description: Scientists have identified two new species of large Australian stick insects, including one that lays extraordinary “lidded” eggs never before recorded in the group. The discovery also revealed that a familiar stick insect had been misidentified for decades, showing how much biodiversity may still be hiding in plain sight. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Pink October: Raising awareness about breast cancer
item.description: Breast cancer is the leading cause of cancer-related deaths among women and more than 61,000 cases are diagnosed in France each year. At Paris's Curie Institute, researchers are trying to develop new ways to identify and treat different types of cancers. One trial involves developing so-called “tumors on a chip”: miniature models which are capable of recreating the characteristics of a tumor in vitro outside of their normal biological context. Fuente: France 24 - English.

item.title: This new qubit could be 100 times less error-prone in superfluid quantum computer breakthrough
item.description: A proposed qubit made with superfluid helium could cut quantum computing error rates by around 100 times by shielding quantum information from common forms of electromagnetic noise. If experiments confirm the predictions, the technology could eventually work alongside today’s superconducting qubits or serve as a new kind of quantum memory. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: This light-powered AI can spot deepfakes with nearly 98% accuracy
item.description: UCLA researchers built an AI system that uses light to analyze more than a dozen videos simultaneously, detecting deepfakes with nearly 98% accuracy. Its speed, low energy demands, and resistance to attacks could make it a powerful tool for screening the growing flood of AI-generated video. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Science or strategy? Researchers call for transparency over the Anthropocene rejection
item.description: Since its introduction in 2000, the concept of the Anthropocene—the idea that human activities are the major driver of Earth systems—has become highly influential throughout society, including in culture, science and law. Yet despite decades of research revealing humanity's influence on the planet, the Anthropocene Working Group's (AWG) proposal of an Anthropocene epoch was ultimately rejected by the International Union of Geological Sciences (IUGS) in 2024. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Gut mRNA tech supercharges vaccine and GLP-1 delivery
item.description: From vaccines to gene therapies, mRNA medicines often rely on tiny fat-based particles called lipid nanoparticles, or LNPs, to carry treatments where they need to go. But researchers still face a fundamental challenge: getting those therapies to the organs where they are needed most while limiting side effects elsewhere in the body. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: New parallel gate entangles diamond qubits 10 times faster at room temperature
item.description: Quantum technologies rely on qubits, units of information that can exist in combinations of the states 0 and 1 instead of being limited to one or the other like conventional bits. Qubits can become entangled, which means their states become linked in ways that cannot be explained by considering each qubit separately. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Why do pickles glow? Researcher investigates explosive answer
item.description: If you mount a pickle on two metal forks and plug it into a socket, one end will light up in a brilliant orange glow. It's a classic K–12 science demonstration, but the exact physics behind the illumination has long remained a mystery. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: What happened this month at the European Space Agency? (September 2026)
item.description: Video: 00:03:32 September was a month of milestones and discoveries. FLEX launched aboard Vega-C alongside Sentinel-3C. Sophie Adenot completed her third and final spacewalk, leading the mission as EV-1. BepiColombo separated from its Mercury Transfer Module, taking another step towards Mercury. Spectrum became the first rocket to reach orbit from continental Europe. And the James Webb Space Telescope found tiny brown dwarfs that could harbor the building blocks of planets. Here’s a look at what space had in store for Europe this September! Fuente: European Space Agency.

item.title: Anti-South Asian online hate surges in US under Trump 2.0, study finds
item.description: Anti-South Asian hate in the United States has spiked since Donald Trump returned to the Oval Office for a second term, with racist, dehumanising and xenophobic slurs and narratives proliferating across both mainstream and fringe social media platforms, a US-based report has revealed. The report, titled “The Rising Tide of Anti-South Asian Hate in the United States”, by the Washington-based Centre for the Study of Organised Hate (CSOH), found that the monthly volume of hate towards South Asians... Fuente: South China Morning Post.
item.dc:creator: Junaid Kathju

item.title: This diet may slow brain aging by 2.5 years
item.description: People who followed the MIND diet more closely showed slower brain shrinkage and less grey matter loss over time, with the strongest differences equivalent to about 2.5 years of delayed brain aging. Berries and poultry were linked with healthier brain changes, while sweets and fried fast foods were associated with greater tissue loss. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: How Trump's AI-generated memes impact political authority and masculinity
item.description: A new article by sociologists Tristan Bridges (University of California, Santa Barbara) and James W. Messerschmidt (University of Southern Maine) examines how AI-generated memes circulated on social media by President Donald Trump represent a significant transformation in the visual politics of masculinity. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: 1 in 13 adults under 30 already had hidden artery plaque
item.description: More than half of 16,000 apparently healthy adults had signs of atherosclerosis, with arterial plaques already detectable in about 1 in 13 people ages 18 to 29. Researchers say directly imaging the arteries could reveal hidden cardiovascular disease years or even decades before symptoms appear. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Navigating tough conversations with people who have dementia about stopping driving
item.description: At some point, all people with dementia must stop driving due to the impact of cognitive impairment on skills critical for safe driving—but when is the right time, and how should this sensitive matter be best approached? Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: The hidden pressure behind responding to a boss's good news
item.description: Have you ever found yourself listening to someone share their good news and felt pressure to respond with excitement, even if you didn't feel particularly enthusiastic? Does that pressure feel even greater when the person sharing the news is your boss? Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: NASA squeezed Treasury, vibe coded, and broke the mold in bid to save Swift
item.description: "We did some really, really cool stuff. I'm absolutely gutted we weren't able to get further." Fuente: Ars Technica.

item.title: Empty nets in Latin America as fish flee El Niño
item.description: Fishermen along Latin America's Pacific coast are reeling in half-empty nets as ocean warming aggravated by El Niño causes tuna, anchovies and other top catches to migrate to cooler waters. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Study shows how research can change person conducting it
item.description: In 2012, I began an interview study with two multilingual language learners, focusing on their motivations for learning languages. It eventually developed into a nine-year longitudinal study. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: EarthCARE’s view of volcanic plume boosts air safety
item.description: When Anak Krakatau erupted a few weeks ago, the European Space Agency’s EarthCARE satellite, orbiting above, captured vertical profiles of different constituents within the volcanic plume. Designed primarily to advance our understanding of how clouds and aerosols influence Earth’s climate, here EarthCARE also provided valuable information to support safe air travel. At the same time, these observations offer new insights into the impact that volcanic eruptions have on the climate system. Fuente: European Space Agency.

item.title: Dos astronautas atrapados nueve meses, cinco propulsores averiados y fugas de helio. Y aun así la NASA sigue confiando en la Starliner
item.description: Los primeros viajes al espacio de la Boeing Starliner no fueron precisamente idílicos . Tras varios fallos en los intentos sin tripular, la NASA consideró que había garantías para emprender un trayecto con tripulación. Afortunadamente los dos astronautas llegaron a la Estación Espacial Internacional (EEI), pero hubo tantas incidencias que se consideró que el viaje de vuelta podría ser peligroso, así que la nave se trajo a la Tierra vacía y sus tripulantes tuvieron que esperar 9 meses en la EEI hasta poder regresar en una cápsula de SpaceX. Después de todo, sería esperable que la NASA haya… Fuente: Xataka.
item.dc:creator: Azucena Martín

item.title: Could quitting ultra-processed food boost your mental health?
item.description: People with depression who dramatically cut ultra-processed foods experienced notable improvements in their symptoms in a small preliminary study. Researchers suspect healthier eating may benefit the brain partly by reducing gut damage and chronic inflammation. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Rice work: Dutch test new crop to save sinking peatlands
item.description: In a soggy field between Amsterdam and The Hague, farmer Sander Roeleveld plows a small white combine harvester into his crops, gathering a grain never before harvested in the Netherlands: rice. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Indonesia haze chokes neighbors, but little legal recourse
item.description: Haze from Indonesian wildfires has blanketed neighboring Malaysia and Singapore for more than a month, closing schools and sending respiratory complaints skyrocketing. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Where does body fat go when we lose weight? The answer is stranger than you expect
item.description: Researchers estimate that around 84% of lost body fat is exhaled as carbon dioxide, while the remaining 16% is lost as water. Fuente: Euronews.

item.title: Resucitar el SR-71 Blackbird suena a locura. Cada vez más pistas apuntan a que la NASA se lo está planteando
item.description: Hace unos días, las redes echaron fuego después de que el administrador de la NASA, Jared Isaacman, mostrase en una conferencia la silueta de lo que parecía el SR-71 Blackbird, uno de los aviones más emblemáticos de la NASA. Esta aeronave supersónica perteneció en primer lugar a la Fuerza Aérea de Estados Unidos. Sin embargo, después de trabajar en numerosas misiones de espionaje, pasó a manos de la agencia espacial, que lo usó como plataforma de investigación durante la década de 1990. Uno de los últimos Blackbirds que se usaron, el número 844, había permanecido expuesto desde entonces en el… Fuente: Xataka.
item.dc:creator: Azucena Martín

item.title: Alzheimer’s risk gene APOE4 may have a reversible weakness
item.description: The Alzheimer’s risk gene APOE4 may actively damage brain blood vessels and sabotage the cellular systems that remove harmful proteins. Researchers were able to reverse some of these effects in experiments, revealing promising new targets for Alzheimer’s, Parkinson’s, and other neurodegenerative diseases. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: 90-plus-day spaceflights linked to higher rates of hip fractures in astronauts
item.description: New research has found that the rate of hip fractures among astronauts after spaceflights lasting more than 90 days was higher than after shorter spaceflights or among people who were not astronauts. The findings of the study in Mayo Clinic Proceedings, underscore the need for expanded assessment of astronauts' long-term skeletal health. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.description: APOD Science APOD APOD: 2026 October 1 –… Today’s APOD Archive Submissions Index Search Calendar RSS Education About Discuss APOD Astronomy Picture of the Day Discover the cosmos! Each day a different image or photograph of our fascinating universe is featured, along with a brief explanation written by a professional astronomer. Harvest Moon with […] Fuente: NASA.

item.title: ‘Explosion of melt rates’: 20% of Swiss glaciers lost in five years
item.description: Alpine regions in Europe experiencing extreme glacier collapse due to heat-trapping effects of fossil fuel pollution Switzerland has lost almost one-fifth of its ice in just five years, research has found, in a dramatic reshaping of the Alpine country whose big white glaciers have been reduced to moonlike rock deserts, scientists say. Swiss glaciers shrank by 5.5% in the first eight months of 2026, according to an annual monitoring report, after a summer of scorching heatwaves that followed a winter with little snow. The reduction in ice volume falls just shy of the record set in 2022 and… Publicado también por: The Guardian - Environment. Fuente: The Guardian - World.
item.dc:creator: Ajit Niranjan

item.title: Women astronauts use social media to reframe science and femininity together
item.description: Why can't a flight jacket be pink or purple? That was the question a 6-year-old girl asked her mother, Kellie Gerardi, an astronaut, researcher and science communicator. When Gerardi later appeared in a TV interview wearing a bright pink flight jacket, her daughter pointed to her mom on the TV screen, smiling with delight. This exchange—which appeared in a post on Gerardi's Instagram account—was a personal moment, skillfully presented through the language and visuals of social media. But it also conveys a clear message: Femininity and scientific credibility are not mutually exclusive. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: An Agricultural “Island” in the Saskatchewan River Delta
item.description: Surrounded by wetlands, Manitoba’s northernmost farmland near The Pas turns from green to brown over the 2026 growing season. Fuente: NASA.

item.title: Caltech physicists finally measure a quantum energy ladder predicted 40 years ago
item.description: Researchers have experimentally observed energy patterns that physicists have predicted for about 40 years. By arranging laser-trapped atoms into a quantum simulator, they recreated two different quantum tipping points and watched the atoms fall into the exact energy ratios predicted by theory. The technique could now be used to explore mysterious quantum systems where scientists do not already know the answer. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Wildlife tracking to fill gaps in monarch migration research
item.description: Every fall, monarch butterflies fuel up on nectar from Iowa's fall-blooming wildflowers before embarking on an extraordinary migration from North America to Mexico. But the pathways they take and how their travel is affected by weather and other factors have largely remained a mystery. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: This common mistake can add nearly 7 points to your blood pressure reading
item.description: A common mistake during blood pressure checks could make readings appear substantially higher than they really are. Johns Hopkins researchers found that leaving the arm unsupported can raise systolic readings by about 6.5 mmHg, potentially affecting a hypertension diagnosis. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Hollywood se sacude: una jueza aprueba la histórica fusión de Warner Bros. Discovery con Paramount
item.description: Una jueza federal aprobó el miércoles 30 de septiembre un acuerdo que autoriza la adquisición de Warner Bros. Discovery por parte de Paramount, luego de que doce estados de EE. UU. impugnaran la operación. El acuerdo incluye garantías para la independencia editorial de 'CNN' y exige que el estudio resultante de la fusión estrene al menos 30 películas al año en sus dos primeros años. La compra ha sido rechazada por figuras de Hollywood que la consideran una amenaza a la industria. Fuente: France 24 - Español.

item.title: Philippines’ uranium find a ‘vital’ boost for nuclear energy ambitions
item.description: Researchers have identified a potential source of uranium in a long-explored mining district in the southern Philippines, as Manila moves to establish nuclear power and expand its critical minerals industry. The discovery, which could provide uranium for the nuclear fuel cycle if further exploration confirms its viability, was made in the Larap-Paracale mining district in Camarines Norte province, where exploration began in the 1950s. Researchers from the Philippine Nuclear Research Institute... Fuente: South China Morning Post.

item.description: "The Traitors" has become essential viewing for millions of fans. The TV game show, in which a group of "faithfuls" try to identify a smaller number of hidden traitors, is all about truth and lies. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.description: A chance and "extremely rare" discovery in an outback fossil pit has uncovered an unknown bird species from more than a hundred million years ago. Fuente: ABC News Australia.

item.title: Fine-tuning cobalt for cleaner chemical transformations
item.description: Finding alternatives to precious metals in chemical manufacturing may be less like sourcing a substitute and more like tuning an instrument already in hand. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Curiosity Blog, Sols 5016–5021: Fantastic Minerals and How To Detect Them
item.description: Written by Lucy Lim, Planetary Scientist at NASA Goddard Space Flight Center Earth planning date: Friday, Sept. 18, 2026 Curiosity surprised us at the beginning of the week with a change in rock texture — instead of the finely layered bedrock blocks we’ve been seeing in our recent sulfate unit workspaces, suddenly we were looking […] Fuente: NASA.

item.title: Bacteria can make plant-based foods healthier for humans and animals
item.description: New research from the DTU National Food Institute and Aarhus University shows that microorganisms can be used to specifically alter the amino acid composition of plant-based foods, making them more nutritious and therefore healthier. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Why some Ukrainian refugees struggle to rebuild their careers after arriving in Canada
item.description: The Russian invasion of Ukraine continues into 2026, with millions of Ukrainians displaced around the world. Many arrived in host countries with professional experience, degrees and specialized skills. Yet displacement often leaves highly educated refugees unable to continue their previous careers. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Scientists develop 'floating scarecrow' to protect threatened seabirds
item.description: New research has shown that a "floating scarecrow" developed by U.K.-based scientists and a repurposed bird-scaring kite can help save threatened seabirds from getting caught in fishing nets. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Community-led archaeology project uncovers a major monastery of medieval Scotland
item.description: Community-led archaeology has uncovered the remains of an early medieval monastery in Argyll, western Scotland, identifying it as the high-ranking ecclesiastical center of Lios Mòr, previously known only from historical references and local traditions. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Devastating year for Switzerland's glaciers after extreme heat and low snow
item.description: Switzerland's glaciers lost more than 5% of their ice volume in 2026. Although melt rates did not quite reach the record levels of 2022, glacier thickness decreased by an average of 2.5 to 4 meters (8 to 13 feet) this year, and some glacier tongues lost up to 10 meters (33 feet) of ice. The research is published in the journal GLAMOS—Glacier Monitoring Switzerland. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Confronting demons: How acoustic and AI technology brought ancient Etruscan tombs back to life
item.description: Although it is not always obvious, sound guides how we experience the world around us. And the latest archaeoacoustic techniques show that even the world's earliest architects understood this. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Key protein for cells' gene regulation needs a chaperone to do its job
item.description: A protein that's essential to every cell's ability to turn off unnecessary genes is well known for its key function of compacting genes and its connection to cancer when it undergoes mutation. But until now, scientists weren't quite sure how the protein gets where it needs to go to keep genes bound up so they aren't activated. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Peruvian mummies raise questions about Wari conquest of Nasca civilization
item.description: For centuries, historians have drawn the boundaries of where ancient people lived based on the evidence they left behind. By studying their remains, burial practices and other archaeological clues, they can determine the types of relationships they had with other people in the area. However, this can all change when new archaeological evidence is found. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: The real cost of coal mines to people and planet
item.description: The longer it takes to transition away from fossil fuels such as coal, the more costs accrue as climate change accelerates. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Ocean predator chemical cues could provide early warnings for toxic algal blooms
item.description: A team of marine scientists led by researchers at the University of California, Santa Cruz, has developed a new approach to predicting harmful algal blooms (HABs), changing how oceanographers track these hazardous marine events. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Catch a rare lunar occultation of Jupiter plus Saturn at opposition in early October
item.description: It's a busy skywatching month ahead. The first full week of October sees two top-notch skywatching events, with Saturn reaching opposition and the moon occulting Jupiter for North America on Oct. 6. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Fluorescent sensors could help researchers see diabetes in action
item.description: Researchers from the University of Bath have developed fluorescent molecular probes that can detect changes in glucose levels inside living animals, giving scientists new ways of visualizing sugar uptake and studying diabetes, cancer and other metabolic diseases in whole organisms in real time. The findings are published in the journal Advanced Science. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Digging deep, researchers find high-altitude glacier endured last ice age
item.description: Ice cores recovered from an ice cap in northwestern Tibet appear to preserve fragments of ancient ice from the last ice age, extending Earth's glacial record by more than 100,000 years and making them the oldest ice cores ever recovered from the region, according to a new study. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: AI scientist autonomously generates and validates new biological discoveries
item.description: Researchers at Chalmers University of Technology in Sweden have developed an AI scientist capable of generating scientific hypotheses, designing experiments and interpreting results. Making new biological discoveries with minimal human intervention is an important advance in self-driving laboratories. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Short on time? It could be good for you
item.description: When it comes to mental health, it may not be how much time you have that matters, but rather how you feel about the time you have. That's one key takeaway of a new University of Colorado Boulder study examining the relationship between time and mental health. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Tracking the fin whale and the sperm whale in the Mediterranean
item.description: Where are the great marine animals of the Mediterranean, such as the fin whale, the sperm whale or the bottlenose dolphin? How does their distribution change over a few weeks? All indications suggest that these species shift between marine areas in a remarkably short time and over relatively small spatial scales. Some species, such as the striped dolphin, maintain a relatively stable presence in certain areas, while others, such as the fin whale, move and concentrate in different areas from one observation campaign to the next. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Anti-fibrotic drug could be repurposed to control cell communication
item.description: An experimental antifibrotic compound can dramatically alter how cells release the microscopic packages they use to communicate, according to new research from the University of Surrey. Researchers found that the compound, SD-208, which reduces scar tissue in organs, substantially reduced the release of extracellular vesicles, microscopic packages that cells use to carry proteins and other biological signals to neighboring and distant cells. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Help Overlap Zoo Reveal Cosmic Dust
item.description: Galaxies, vast collections of billions of stars, gas, and dust held together by gravity, are scattered across the immensity of space. But every so often, a coincidence occurs: Two galaxies line up from our point of view on Earth (or from a space telescope) and appear to overlap in the sky. These rare overlapping galaxies […] Fuente: NASA.

item.title: NASA Adds New Science Investigations for Moon Base
item.description: Editor’s note: This release was updated on Sept. 30, 2026, to correct the name of the DISCO payload. NASA selected three new scientific investigations and their payload suites to advance our knowledge of the Moon and help pave the way for building humanity’s first lunar outpost, Moon Base. The suite of science instruments and technologies […] Fuente: NASA.

item.title: Scientists in 1960 predicted Friday 13 November 2026 will be 'Doomsday.' Should you be worried?
item.description: In 1960, Science, one of the world's leading science journals, published an article with an unambiguous title: Doomsday: Friday, 13 November, A.D. 2026. It predicted that on this future date—just over a month from today—the human population would approach infinity and effectively annihilate itself. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: 1 in 2 Florida residents live in HOAs—how these private governments are reshaping the American Dream
item.description: As she sat across from me drinking tea, Coretta—a pseudonym to protect her identity—shared her dismay about living in a central Florida community because of the control exercised by her homeowners association, or HOA. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Fossil long known as world's oldest reptile dethroned
item.description: For nearly 30 years, a small fossil from Scotland has been celebrated as one of the earliest known reptiles. A new study out today in Nature and led by researchers at the American Museum of Natural History and the University of Oxford, in collaboration with the European Synchrotron Radiation Facility, is rewriting that story. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: 'Molecular movie' fills in blanks of how nonenveloped viruses infect cells
item.description: Viruses come in two major flavors—not chocolate and vanilla, quips Harvard Medical School structural biologist Stephen Harrison, but those enveloped in membranes, such as herpesvirus, influenza virus, HIV and SARS-CoV-2, and those that are not, such as poliovirus, HPV, rotavirus and adenovirus. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: NASA Awards Contract to Develop 5G Communications for Moon
item.description: NASA has awarded Modulate Space Corporation a contract to develop key elements of a 5G communications system for use on the lunar surface with built-in Wi-Fi 6, for NASA’s Glenn Research Center in Cleveland. This accelerated effort is organized into two primary work areas that together will develop a scalable, standards-based communications capability designed to […] Fuente: NASA.

item.title: Clay tablets reveal how Babylonian students learned about their gods
item.description: When it came to religious education in ancient Babylonia, in what is now Iraq, students had a lot to learn, ranging from the names of gods to their divine characteristics. A new study published in the journal Iraq has taken a deep dive into ancient texts and surviving clay tablets to find out just how these traditions were taught in the classroom. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Some threatened species may miss out as zoos try to balance conservation efforts with competing pressures
item.description: In the largest study of its kind, researchers at Nottingham Trent University analyzed more than 7,200 species across 613 zoos in 72 countries over a 30-year period. The team compared changes in zoo animal holdings with changes in species' conservation status, including extinction risk, international trade protections and involvement in zoo conservation breeding programs. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Mouse study reveals magnetic nanoparticles' potential for ectopic pregnancy diagnosis and treatment
item.description: A research team led by an Oregon State University scientist has demonstrated in a mouse model a potentially better way to care for women facing the life-threatening condition of ectopic pregnancy. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Wood beneath German lake may reveal buildings 3,000 years older than region's first farms
item.description: Underwater archaeological investigations have been taking place in Lake Arendsee (Altmarkkreis Salzwedel) for several years. The discovery of Neolithic fish weirs, a high medieval barge (flat-bottomed cargo ship) and a late medieval dugout canoe attracted considerable attention. Fuente: Phys.org.
